comparator.name: Philosophy
comparator.sourceNotes: Reconstructed from the official Onderwijs- en Examenregeling bachelor Filosofie 2026-2027, using Appendix 2B for the full-time cohort starting in 2026-2027. The formal curriculum comprises two fixed 60-EC years followed by a 15-EC non-philosophy minor, 15 EC of Advanced Academic Skills choices, Filosofie in de Praktijk, one 7.5-EC philosophy elective and the 15-EC Bachelor Thesis. Where the current public study-programme page differs from the formal curriculum overview, the OER governs this reconstruction: public-page subjects that are absent from Appendix 2A are not treated as 2026-2027 curriculum. The separate RASL double-study arrangement is not the normalized target reconstructed here, and the programme has no formal routes or specialisations requiring a route choice. The two Advanced Academic Skills slots take the first two of the three options in the order Appendix 2A lists them — Wittgenstein and Philosophies of Information and Computation — as a neutral tie-break fixed independently of the UCR side. The year-3 philosophy elective remains Contemporary Thought of Technology, a valid option in Appendix 2A that is also presented on the current public study-programme page. The 15-EC minor or exchange space is genuine non-philosophy profiling space and is preserved rather than filled with invented content. Admission to bachelor years 2 and 3 normally requires a positive binding study advice; the bachelor thesis requires 90 EC completed within the Filosofie examination programme.

trace: Examines fairness, privacy, responsibility, alignment, moral status and political risks through ethical theory and psychological perspectives, with a literature-based project and podcast. Directly contributes AI ethics; interpretability or a specialised philosophy-of-information syllabus is not assumed.

Develops propositional and quantified logic, proof, sets, Boolean algebra, functions, induction and recursion, then formal modelling of games without chance. Directly supports logical argument; mathematical applications complement philosophical reasoning.
examines how information is modelled, structured, stored and queried, which is the concrete substance behind philosophical claims about information and computation
introduces data practice and the computational handling of information that a philosophy of information has to engage with concretely
provides working knowledge of the machine-learning models whose behaviour and limits the programme evaluates
examines neural network architectures and deep learning, the specific technology behind current claims about artificial intelligence
supplies the mathematical methods required for the later formal and machine-learning work
examines recycling, recovery and remediation as material responses to environmental harm
analyses how sustainability is governed, regulated and contested across institutions
explains how ecosystems function, which the value claims made about nature presuppose

Investigates nuclear waste storage, geothermal energy and CO2 capture through geoscience literature research, class reports and a professional-conference presentation. These resource and environmental cases give concrete scientific constraints for environmental responsibility; no dedicated theory of resource justice is assumed.

Introduces planetary boundaries, physical and chemical sustainability processes, uncertainty and dynamic models, with a biopolymer laboratory project. Provides concrete environmental-science foundations for evaluating sustainability claims.

Develops wave physics, chemical analysis and material properties, with laboratory work and critical assessment of sustainability campaigns and greenwashing. It supplies scientific and evaluative tools for the environmental-practice concept.
provides the climate science whose consequences the moral argument is about
analyses life-cycle assessment and circular-economy design as concrete sustainability practice
trains systematic detection of misinformation, pseudoscience and statistical manipulation and the assessment of scientific credibility
requires the design of renewable systems, grounding normative debate in technical feasibility

Small teams investigate partner-defined sustainability problems using literature review, research design and a final product or report. This is collaborative applied research, not an individual philosophical thesis; the project topic is not predetermined.
gives the chronological account of the modern period in which popular sovereignty, Marxism, socialism and liberal political ideals took shape
examines the body, lived experience and power through the histories of gender, drawing on hooks and Crenshaw
studies human rights legally, historically and philosophically, from the classical declarations to contemporary treaties
provides the systematic introduction to Western philosophical questions, arguments and traditions on which the later philosophical work depends

Develops utilitarian, Kantian, virtue, contractarian and feminist ethics through close reading, argument evaluation and independent essays. Directly supplies moral-theory foundations; environmental topics and their weight are not assumed from an older syllabus.
examines consciousness, personal identity, the mind-body problem and machine consciousness as philosophical problems
analyses emotion and affect philosophically, including their relation to rationality, value and well-being
treats free will, time, agency and the self as advanced metaphysical problems

Studies European and non-European political thought, human nature, society, rights and authority through original texts, essays and a group political-philosophy project. Directly supports normative political inquiry.

Develops qualitative research design, ethics, positionality, interviews, ethnography and documentary or visual approaches, with coding and interpretation. Complements philosophical questions about knowledge with an actual empirical inquiry method; it is not a systematic epistemology course.
traces the development of sociology and social theory through modernity, imperialism and colonial responses
studies environmental justice movements and collective action on ecological harm
deepens the study of memory, attention, executive function and cognitive control that philosophy of mind treats conceptually
studies how language is acquired, produced and understood, giving empirical substance to philosophical questions about language and mind
provides the foundational account of brain and behaviour that the programme's later mind and language courses build on
analyses rhetorical argument through ethos, pathos and logos and requires students to construct and evaluate persuasive cases
develops close stylistic reading, showing how linguistic choices create meaning and carry ideological weight
examines how climate knowledge is communicated, framed and contested in public debate
examines theories of persuasion and applies them to contemporary public argument
examines modern art and the museum institutions that frame it, connecting aesthetic judgment to its historical and institutional setting
trains close reading and interpretation across narrative and non-fiction forms
compares humanist, feminist, Marxist, cultural-minority and psychoanalytic perspectives on interpretation and requires students to apply them to texts
provides the foundation in film and media analysis, including how media technologies shape perception and cultural production
examines pre-digital media technologies and how they shaped the production, circulation and preservation of knowledge

Studies American everyday life, storytelling, power and representation through television, film and digital media, including Indigenous and disability perspectives. Provides concrete cases for evaluating technological mediation and imagined futures, rather than a generic platform-economy course.
examines how environmental change is represented and mediated
examines how racial meaning is produced and contested in media representation
studies documentary form and its claims to truth, evidence and representation

alternatives.label: Philosophy, ethics & the human sciences
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is not a philosophy curriculum alone. It combines the five UCR philosophy courses and political philosophy with history, sociology, literary study, rhetoric, cognitive science and formal logic, because that is where UCR teaches the material a philosophy bachelor covers within its own discipline. The label therefore names both the philosophical core and the human-science fields through which the rest of that ground is reached, rather than presenting the programme as a full philosophy degree.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to a full philosophy bachelor: the philosophical core of ethics, mind, metaphysics, political philosophy and logic, extended through the fields in which UCR teaches the history of ideas, social theory, textual interpretation and the empirical study of mind and language.
progression: Current planned offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked for every placement. Philosophical introductions, brain and behaviour, sustainability foundations and introductory data work precede dependent advanced study where applicable; advisory progression was considered without inventing additional prerequisites.
traceOverrides: places modern art within the history of ideas and requires interpretation of works and of the institutions that frame them
applies moral theory to a concrete contemporary domain — fairness, interpretability and human flourishing — as applied ethics rather than as a technology direction of its own
examines how documentary form makes and defends claims to truth and evidence, which is where contemporary argument about knowledge and expertise is conducted publicly

alternatives.label: Philosophy, technology, media & artificial intelligence
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum pairs the philosophical core with media study and with genuine technical work in data science, machine learning, deep learning and data management. The label names philosophy alongside the technology and media strands rather than describing the whole programme as philosophy of technology, since much of it is data science and media studies in their own right.
alternatives.concept: A programme organised around the philosophical and ethical evaluation of technology, information and artificial intelligence: the philosophical core is retained, and the elective space goes to media theory and to the technical study of the systems whose claims and effects are being assessed.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this route drops the human-science strand — Modern History, Modern Sociology, Histories of Gender, Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Higher Order Functions, Psycholinguistics, Introduction to Literary Studies, Style & Meaning, Modern Art & Modern Museums and Introduction to Political Philosophy — and replaces it with media archaeology, film and media analysis, platform media, media and race, documentary, and a technical sequence running from Introduction to Data Science through Machine Learning to Neural Networks & Deep Learning. The educational choice is different in kind: the student evaluates technology with working knowledge of how it is built, rather than studying mind and society through the human sciences. Ten of the 24 courses differ.
progression: Current planned offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked for every placement. Philosophical introductions, brain and behaviour, sustainability foundations and introductory data work precede dependent advanced study where applicable; advisory progression was considered without inventing additional prerequisites.

alternatives.label: Ethics, sustainability & environmental practice
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum is an ethics programme grounded in actual environmental science, governance and engineering practice: climate science, life-cycle analysis, ecosystems, remediation, renewable design and sustainability governance sit alongside the philosophical core. The label states that combination rather than calling the programme philosophy of sustainability, which would overstate the philosophical share.
alternatives.concept: A programme organised around what we owe to nature, to future generations and to each other: moral and political philosophy applied to environmental practice, with the sustainability science, governance and technology that the normative questions are about.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this route keeps the ethical and political core but replaces the entire human-science and interpretive strand — Introduction to Literary Studies, Perspectives on Literary Meaning, Style & Meaning, Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Higher Order Functions, Psycholinguistics, Philosophy of Mind, AI Ethics, Modern History, Histories of Gender, Modern Art & Modern Museums and Logic & Discrete Mathematics — with the two sustainability gateways, climate science, life-cycle analysis, ecosystems, remediation, renewable system design, sustainability governance, environmental justice, climate communication and delta research. Compared with the technology route it shares only the philosophical core and the method courses. The student here argues about environmental obligations from inside the technical and governance practice being judged. Twelve of the 24 courses differ from the closest match and fourteen from the technology route.
progression: Current planned offerings and earlier formal prerequisites checked for every placement. Philosophical introductions, brain and behaviour, sustainability foundations and introductory data work precede dependent advanced study where applicable; advisory progression was considered without inventing additional prerequisites.
traceOverrides: Provides interviews, ethnography, reflexivity and interpretive analysis for investigating how communities understand environmental responsibility.

selection.assessment: The closest match owns the twelve generator-eligible interests that describe philosophy as a discipline — fundamental questions, truth and knowledge, what it is to be human, critical and logical thinking, argument, close reading, the history of ideas, contemporary philosophy in public debate, justice, the analytic and continental traditions, existential questions and the good life. The two remaining generator-eligible interests each define a coherent direction of its own: the philosophy of technology together with philosophy across medicine, AI and economics, and sustainability and environmental ethics. Both are supported by named components of the current official curriculum — Philosophy of Art, Media & Technology, Contemporary Thought of Technology and the information-and-communication Advanced Academic Skills course for the first; Moral Philosophy and Environmental Practice for the second — and both can be built as valid UCR programmes that differ from the closest match and from each other by well over the four-course floor. Three alternatives are therefore included and the maximum is reached; no further candidate direction was constructed, since every remaining interest row is either a curricular topic supporting these three concepts or a search-only outcome row.

blocks: Human Conditions and Philosophy of Mind both take the philosophical analysis of what it is to be human as their primary subject: consciousness, personal identity and the limits of naturalistic explanation.

Both address moral philosophy and ethical reasoning. UCR provides sustained study of moral theories and independent argument; the Erasmus course explicitly connects moral philosophy with environmental practice.
Both address metaphysical questions. UCR studies free will, agency, time and selfhood through historical and contemporary arguments; it does not reproduce a systematic continental-metaphysics course.

Contemporary Thought of Technology and AI Ethics both examine technology philosophically. UCR's course concentrates that examination on artificial intelligence, fairness, alignment and human flourishing.

Theoretical Analytic Philosophy is a dedicated survey of analytic method and its central problems. No single UCR course occupies that role; the material is spread across Philosophy of Mind, Free Will, Time & the Self and Logic & Discrete Mathematics, so the component is left unmatched rather than forced onto one of them.

What Can We Know? is a systematic epistemology course running from antiquity to the modern age. UCR offers no epistemology course, and Introduction to Western Philosophy — which touches these questions — is the counterpart of the Rotterdam introduction rather than of this one.
Filosofie in Nederland studies the Dutch philosophical tradition specifically. UCR has no counterpart and none is manufactured.

Both develop formal logical reasoning. UCR explicitly teaches propositional and quantified logic, proof, sets and induction, with additional mathematical and game-modelling applications; it does not reproduce the complete philosophical-logic course.

Philosophy of Science is a dedicated course on scientific knowledge, method and explanation. UCR has no philosophy-of-science course. Calling Bullshit trains the evaluation of evidence and scientific credibility but is a critical-thinking course rather than a philosophical treatment of science, so the component is left unmatched.

Filosofie in de Praktijk places philosophical skills in professional practice. UCR's Personal & Professional Development serves a different purpose — personal formation and academic-skills development, without the disciplinary content — so the component is recorded as unmatched rather than equated with it.

Historisering van het Wereldbeeld and Modern History both study how worldviews were historically formed and transformed; the UCR course does so through the political and intellectual history of the modern period from 1815.
Geschiedenis, Maatschappij en Individu and Modern Sociology both examine the relation between society and the individual through social theory and the history of modernity.

Both address bodies, experience and power. UCR studies these through North American gender histories, intersectionality and primary-source research; it is a partial historical relationship to the philosophical component.

Politics and Critique and Introduction to Political Philosophy are both the programme's political-philosophy component, examining political authority, society and critique through influential thinkers.

Enlightenment is a dedicated study of Enlightenment philosophy. Modern History begins in 1815 and is already the counterpart of Historisering van het Wereldbeeld, so no UCR course covers this period philosophically and the gap is preserved.

Taal en Geest and Psycholinguistics both address the relation between language and mind. The Rotterdam course does so philosophically and the UCR course through the neurobiological and psychological study of language acquisition, production and comprehension; the primary subject is the same.

Wittgenstein is a dedicated advanced seminar on one philosopher and his work on language, logic and meaning. UCR addresses some related questions in broader philosophy and language courses but offers no dedicated Wittgenstein or philosophy-of-language course, so the component remains unmatched.

Philosophy of Art, Media & Technology and Introduction to Film & Media share art, media and technology as their subject, including how media technologies shape perception and cultural production; the UCR course is an analytical rather than a philosophical treatment.

Philosophies of Information and Computation treats information and computation as philosophical subjects. UCR offers technical computing, formal logic and AI-ethics courses, but none centres on the philosophy of information and computation, so the component remains unmatched rather than being equated with applied technical study.

The Rotterdam programme reserves 15 EC of genuine non-philosophy profiling space as a minor or exchange period. UCR programmes are composed entirely of 7.5-EC courses and have no equivalent reserved block, so the space is shown as it stands.
The Bachelor Thesis Filosofie is a 15-EC supervised independent philosophical study. None of the 24 scheduled UCR courses is a thesis, so the component is recorded as unmatched.

notes.text: The Rotterdam programme is a full philosophy curriculum: a systematic sequence in the history of philosophy, epistemology, metaphysics, logic, philosophy of science, philosophy of language and mind, moral and political philosophy, closing with a 15-EC philosophical thesis. UCR teaches five philosophy courses — Introduction to Western Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind, Philosophy of Emotion, and Free Will, Time & the Self — together with Introduction to Political Philosophy, Human Rights: Law & Philosophy and AI Ethics. At UCR the remaining philosophical ground is approached through neighbouring fields: the history of ideas through history, social critique through sociology, interpretation through literary study and rhetoric, and mind and language through cognitive science. These programmes therefore offer related perspectives on philosophical questions rather than reproducing a full philosophy curriculum, and UCR has no dedicated epistemology, philosophy of science or single-philosopher course.

audience.programmeDescription: Philosophy at Erasmus University Rotterdam is a full philosophy bachelor spanning historical and contemporary traditions, logic, epistemology, metaphysics, ethics, political philosophy, mind and language, philosophy of science, art and technology, advanced academic skills and a 15-EC philosophical thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: Three UCR programmes offer related study through philosophy with the human sciences; philosophy with technology, media and artificial intelligence; or ethics with sustainability and environmental practice. Each keeps a substantial philosophical spine, but UCR does not reproduce Erasmus's complete specialist sequence in epistemology, philosophy of science, continental metaphysics, philosophy of language, single-philosopher study or a philosophy thesis.

curriculum.limitation: This 2026–2027 pathway includes a 15-EC non-philosophy minor, two Advanced Academic Skills choices, Contemporary Thought of Technology as the philosophy elective, and a 15-EC thesis. Years 2 and 3 normally require a positive binding study advice; the thesis requires 90 EC completed within the Philosophy programme.
